USS Constitution. The oldest naval vessel still in commission, a 44-gun wooden frigate launched in 1797 that earned the nickname "Old Ironsides" during the War of 1812 for her seeming invulnerability to cannon fire. She became a symbol of American naval power and ingenuity in the early republic.

Constitution was designed by Joshua Humphreys with revolutionary hull construction using diagonal bracing and thick oak planking. She served in the Barbary Wars from 1801 to 1805, seeing extensive action against North African pirate states threatening American merchant ships. Her most famous engagement came in 1812, when she defeated the British frigate HMS Guerrière in a dramatic single-ship action where British cannon balls reportedly bounced off her hull, giving her the enduring nickname "Old Ironsides."

She remained in active service through the Mexican-American War and Civil War era before being mothballed and restored as a national memorial. Still berthed in Boston Harbor, she remains the oldest commissioned warship in the world. Her hull has been fully restored and she occasionally ventures on ceremonial cruises. Her innovative design influenced frigate construction globally and proved American shipwright innovations in durability and speed. As a masterpiece of wooden ship construction at the peak of sail-powered naval technology, she stands as foundational to the early U.S. Navy's reputation for superior seamanship and ship design.
